article.title: Trumpism Is Running Out of Gas
article.author: Luke Savage
article.content: I have no special insight into what the exact outcome of this yearʼs midterm elections is going to be. It would be absolutely astonishing if Democrats failed to take the House, and the latest NY/Sienna poll has the Democrats leading in all seven of the races that will determine control of the Senate. This includes nonnegligible edges in both Texas and Kansas, the latter of which hasnʼt elected a Democratic senator since the early 1930s. In Michigan, which has been getting a great deal of attention for obvious reasons , Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed boasts a double digit lead, and several key gubernatorial races look to be leaning the same way. Donald Trumpʼs approval rating, meanwhile, is catastrophically low and has been dropping steadily. If Democrats donʼt make considerable gains across the board tonight, it will mean major polling companies got things badly wrong. For other reasons that are less strictly related to polling, however, it has increasingly seemed to me that Trumpism is out of gas and may soon be on its last legs. To reiterate something that cannot be repeated enough: Trump has never been particularly popular. So it was wrongheaded for shocked liberal commentators to throw up their hands and declare the country lost , both in 2016 and 2024. In order to consolidate its hold on the countryʼs politics, the Trump project ultimately needed to mobilize a larger popular coalition — something it has consistently proven unable to do. In his second term especially, in fact, Trump has often seemed indifferent to public opinion and has looked visibly unconcerned when it comes to selling the administrationʼs direction to voters. (I wrote about this back in April specifically in relation to the US-Israeli attack on Iran, though there are certainly other examples.) Beyond all this, Iʼve been struck by the nature of Trumpʼs midterm campaigning itself. CNN recently published an interesting piece in which various reporters reflect on Trump’s rallies theyʼve been attending. Hereʼs how the piece opens: Ballrooms. Cognitive tests. The male physique. As President Donald Trump closes out the midterm election season with a sprint through ruby red America, his message to voters has veered into some unexpected places. More than ever before, his stops have been remarkable because theyʼre about one thing: Trump himself. His message to voters is to pretend heʼs on the ballot, no matter how unpopular heʼs become. Concerns about the direction of the country, or the cost of living, are mostly shoved to the side. Indeed, the substance of Trumpʼs speeches speaks to a political project that is increasingly exhausted and running on fumes. When Trumpism has been politically strongest, its tenor has been insurgent, and it has at least tried to operate in some kind of populist register. It has successfully tapped into generalized anger toward the political class and rightly or wrongly (usually the latter) convinced at least some nontraditional GOP voters it will bring genuine heterodoxy to government. It has, albeit with deep incoherence, attacked the global trade consensus and hinted it will put an end to unpopular wars. It has promised jobs and reindustrialization. It has hit cost-of-living issues hard, even when engaging in more conventional right-wing messaging about immigration and culture war issues. Trumpism has always been profoundly ugly. But here, again, it has found its greatest political success when able to democratize the ugliness somewhat. Its many appeals to racism and sexism have delivered politically when integrated into a larger narrative of hedonism — elect me and you, too, will have license to be nasty and say all the unsayable words again — and national renewal. Here, for example, is an excerpt from Trumpʼs 2016 speech to the Republican National Convention: America is a nation of believers, dreamers, and strivers that is being led by a group of censors, critics, and cynics. Remember: all of the people telling you that you canʼt have the country you want are the same people telling you that I wouldnʼt be standing here tonight. No longer can we rely on those elites in media, and politics, who will say anything to keep a rigged system in place. . . . My opponent asks her supporters to recite a three-word loyalty pledge. It reads: “Iʼm With Her.ˮ I choose to recite a different pledge. My pledge reads: “IʼM WITH YOU — THE AMERICAN PEOPLE.ˮ I am your voice. The contrast between the above and how Trump has been speaking more recently is striking. The rank ugliness that has defined Trump-era conservatism from the beginning remains. Alongside the usual stand-up comedy, however, his midterm campaigning has also featured many moments like these, from the CNN piece: The moment that stood out in Perry, Georgia, on October 24 was Trumpʼs assertion that the United States is “making hundreds and hundreds of billions, trillions of dollarsˮ in oil at a time when people are facing high prices at the pump. Appearing to recognize the disconnect, the president acknowledged his aides had advised him not to mention gas prices and oil. “My people said, ‘please donʼt mention that, sir!ʼˮ he said. Trump said the media would later report that “President Trump is talking about all the money we are making while people are suffering at the pump,ˮ in a kind of self-fulfilling prophecy. “I donʼt give a damn! Iʼm going to say it. Weʼre making a freaking fortune!ˮ he thundered. At both stops on October 27, Trump dangled $5,000 checks for Americans if Republicans win control of the House and Senate. In Corpus Christi, he invited voters to spend their cash payment at Mar-a-Lago — before quipping they wouldnʼt be able to afford it. “You could even come to Mar-a-Lago,ˮ Trump said. “The problem is that for $5,000, the most youʼll be able to buy is a hamburger and maybe a small dessert. Iʼm not even sure you could buy that. No, donʼt go there. Thatʼs not a good place if youʼre price conscious.ˮ Whatever he happens to be talking about — his war with Iran, the cost of living, his redecoration of the White House — Trumpʼs messaging, both on the campaign trail and off, has increasingly resembled the above. Thereʼs no hint of a populist undertone here. Thereʼs not even half-hearted attempt to sell the administrationʼs war with Iran nor any message about the cost of living beyond an emblematically cheeky assurance that everything is actually fine. When Trumpism has been most confident and politically robust, it has categorically not looked or sounded like this. That, to say nothing of the polls, suggests to me that MAGA may really and truly be exhausted and about to suffer a significant body blow. Should that indeed happen, Trump may still be in a position to inflict plenty more harm — but will in all likelihood serve out the remainder of his time in office as a deeply unpopular and fatally compromised figure.
